Summary:
Site Management (SM) implemented an orientation session on Community-Led Initiatives (CLI) as part of Site Management activities, aiming to promote community participation, ownership, and self-reliance by supporting projects that benefit the wider community rather than individuals. The Site Improvement Plan for Al-Awda Site (GZA4195), prepared by BLDA on 10 May 2026, highlights key infrastructure and environmental challenges affecting displaced populations within the site. The plan focuses on improving safety, accessibility, and overall living conditions through targeted site maintenance and improvement interventions.

The main identified issues include:

The presence of random and closely located debris and rubble near tents, which obstruct movement, create environmental and health risks, and contribute to the spread of rodents and insects.
Water accumulation in low-lying areas inside the site due to poor ground leveling, causing movement difficulties and increasing health and safety risks.

To address these challenges, the planned interventions include:

Debris removal, filling works, and ground leveling to improve site conditions and reduce environmental hazards.
Sand spreading and leveling activities to improve drainage, reduce water accumulation, and facilitate safer movement within the site.

These activities are planned to be implemented during May and are expected to require a maximum of 3 working days, using laborers, transportation vehicles, a loader, sand, and leveling tools.

A Site Improvement Plan has been prepared for site GZA4924 (B13) by BLDA on 10 May 2026. It also highlighted the importance of Gender-Based Violence (GBV) prevention and response, focusing on identifying risks, promoting safe practices, and ensuring appropriate referral mechanisms. It also introduces the CFM. Overall, the training aimed to strengthen participants’ capacity to support effective, protection-focused site management.

Topic(s): Communal Space Upgrades, Communal Space Upgrades
Summary: Care and Maintenance Tools Distribution Activity was implemented across 30 IDP sites including this site to address the lack of proper tools required for Cash for works and daily site maintenance, especially in flood-prone areas. The sites were facing challenges in digging drainage channels, removing debris, and maintaining safe pathways during rainy conditions, and also during cleaning the pathways in the site . To mitigate these issues, NRC distributed essential tools including shovels, hoes, pickaxes, wheelbarrows, plastic garden combs, and complete toolboxes. These tools enabled site teams and community workers to carry out regular cleaning, soil excavation, and drainage channel construction more effectively. The intervention also improved preparedness for flooding risks and supported safer and more organized site conditions. Overall, the activity strengthened site maintenance capacity and contributed to improving the living environment for IDPs across the targeted sites.

Al-Nakheel site faces severe WASH, shelter, environmental, and protection risks driven by flooding, high water table, poor sanitation, overcrowding, and lack of lighting and site security.

The proposed intervention aims to reduce protection risks and improve safety through integrated upgrades in WASH, shelter, drainage, and site infrastructure.

Key actions include rehabilitation and construction of safe latrines, proper decommissioning of unsafe pits, improved water supply systems, and establishment of solid waste management and hygiene promotion activities. Shelter improvements will include upgraded transitional shelters, winterization support, site leveling, and better fire safety layout.

Environmental measures will focus on storm-water drainage, vector control, and improved waste management. Protection actions will include installation of solar lighting, fire safety preparedness, and perimeter fencing to enhance overall site safety and security.

The Al-Bawasil Site faces critical WASH, shelter, environmental, and protection challenges, including severe water shortages, degraded sanitation systems, overcrowded and insecure shelters, lack of lighting, and weak site safety measures.

The intervention aims to restore dignity and improve safety by addressing urgent infrastructure gaps and reducing protection risks.

Key actions include improving water supply through communal storage and distribution systems, rehabilitating and upgrading latrines with privacy features, safely managing cesspools, and strengthening solid waste management and hygiene promotion.

Shelter upgrades will focus on installing secure doors, reinforcing structures, reducing overcrowding, and providing winterization support. Environmental works will include drainage systems, vector control, and pathway improvements.

Protection measures will include installation of solar lighting, fire safety preparedness, site fencing, and improved access to support services for vulnerable groups.

The Wijdan Site faces a severe humanitarian crisis affecting 630 families, with critical gaps in WASH, shelter, environmental safety, and protection services.

Major issues include dilapidated and overcrowded latrines, unsafe wastewater disposal, lack of solid waste management, severe pest infestations, and widespread skin diseases. Shelters are highly insecure, overcrowded, and made of weak materials with no proper doors or locks.

The site is also highly vulnerable to flooding due to its low-lying sand dune location, with narrow pathways restricting emergency access. Protection risks are compounded by absence of lighting, fencing, and child-safe or educational spaces.

The intervention aims to improve dignity and safety through latrine rehabilitation with privacy upgrades, installation of secure shelter doors, drainage systems for flood prevention, solar lighting, and establishment of safe learning spaces.

Additional actions include waste management systems, pest control, site reorganization, fire safety measures, and perimeter fencing to enhance overall protection and living conditions.

A Site Management training session was conducted at Al-Shaheed Jameel site targeting members of the Site Management Committee (SMC), with the aim of strengthening their capacity to effectively manage site-level activities and represent the needs of the displaced population. The training provided a comprehensive overview of the Five Core Activities of Site Management, highlighting the importance of coordination, service monitoring, community participation, and accountability within the humanitarian response framework. In addition, the session emphasized the Code of Conduct (CoC), ensuring that committee members clearly understand ethical standards, roles, and expected behaviors while performing their responsibilities. The training also introduced key principles of Protection from Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA), reinforcing the importance of safeguarding vulnerable groups and promoting a safe and respectful environment within the site. Furthermore, detailed explanations were provided regarding the structure of SMCs, including the roles and responsibilities of different committees, to ensure clarity in task distribution and enhance coordination mechanisms. The session was delivered in an interactive and simplified manner to ensure accessibility and understanding, ultimately contributing to improved performance, stronger governance, and more effective service delivery within the site.

Summary: Furniture Distribution (2 Tables, 2 Mats and 9 Chairs per site ) for SMC Activity was implemented to address the lack of proper furniture inside administrative tents across IDP sites, which was affecting communication, coordination, and service delivery. On 7 April 2026, NRC Site Management teams distributed essential furniture to 30 sites across Gaza, the Middle Area, and Khan Younis, including this site. The activity created more organized and dignified spaces for receiving displaced families and conducting daily operations. It also improved complaint handling, referrals, and communication between site management teams and IDPs. In addition, the furnished tents enhanced coordination meetings with community committees and humanitarian partners. Overall, the intervention strengthened service delivery and benefited more than 131,000 displaced individuals across the targeted sites

The planned intervention focuses on debris removal and road widening within the site, as the close accumulation of debris near tents is contributing to the significant spread of rodents, pests, and insects. The activity aims to improve environmental health conditions, facilitate safer movement and accessibility, and enhance the safety of displaced residents.

Topic(s): Communal Space Upgrades, Communal Space Upgrades
Summary: Care and Maintenance Tools Distribution Activity was implemented across 30 IDP sites including this site to address the lack of proper tools required for Cash for works and daily site maintenance, especially in flood-prone areas. The sites were facing challenges in digging drainage channels, removing debris, and maintaining safe pathways during rainy conditions, and also during cleaning the pathways in the site . To mitigate these issues, NRC distributed essential tools including shovels, hoes, pickaxes, wheelbarrows, plastic garden combs, and complete toolboxes. These tools enabled site teams and community workers to carry out regular cleaning, soil excavation, and drainage channel construction more effectively. The intervention also improved preparedness for flooding risks and supported safer and more organized site conditions. Overall, the activity strengthened site maintenance capacity and contributed to improving the living environment for IDPs across the targeted sites.

The sessions included a presentation of project objectives and planned activities, followed by interactive discussions with participants to explore challenges and needs within the sites, as well as discussing the risks faced by residents such as safety concerns, lack of services, and environmental conditions. Dedicated sessions were also conducted with women and girls to ensure their perspectives are included in planning and decision-making.

Overall, the sessions demonstrated positive community engagement and a clear willingness to participate in the implementation of activities and improve living conditions within displacement sites.

Topic: Programming Specific Meetings (e.g. project inductions, cash for work, etc.)
Summary:
Site Management (SM) implemented an orientation session on Community-Led Initiatives (CLI) as part of Site Management activities, aiming to promote community participation, ownership, and self-reliance by supporting projects that benefit the wider community rather than individuals. These initiatives contribute to key objectives such as improving safety, social cohesion, environmental conditions, community services, and group-based livelihoods.

The number and budget of initiatives are defined during the project design stage, while their distribution is determined by the SM team based on needs and context, in coordination with other humanitarian actors to avoid duplication. Site committees serve as the main applicants, ensuring inclusive consultations with community members to identify priorities. Diverse and gender-balanced participation, particularly women’s involvement in leadership roles, is strongly encouraged.

During the session, the mechanism for filling out the Community-Led Initiatives application link was also explained, along with guidance on how to answer the questions included in the form to ensure that applications are submitted clearly and correctly.

Overall, the activity strengthened site maintenance capacity and contributed to improving the living environment for IDPs across the targeted sites.

The sites were facing challenges in digging drainage channels, removing debris, and maintaining safe pathways during rainy conditions, and also during cleaning the pathways in the site . To mitigate these issues, NRC distributed essential tools including shovels, hoes, pickaxes, wheelbarrows, plastic garden combs, and complete toolboxes. Overall, the activity strengthened site maintenance capacity and contributed to improving the living environment for IDPs across the targeted sites.

Summary: Furniture Distribution (2 Tables, 2 Mats and 9 Chairs per site ) for SMC Activity was implemented to address the lack of proper furniture inside administrative tents across IDP sites, which was affecting communication, coordination, and service delivery. On 7 April 2026, NRC Site Management teams distributed essential furniture to 30 sites across Gaza, the Middle Area, and Khan Younis, including this site. The activity created more organized and dignified spaces for receiving displaced families and conducting daily operations. FGD  – Women > 50 Year
The discussion guide examines the roles and responsibilities of women within the community, comparing current conditions with the period before the crisis. It explores daily life, lived experiences, and levels of independence, including reliance on others for routine activities.
It also investigates access to food, non-food items, and essential services, focusing on how resources are obtained, controlled, and whether women have equitable access and decision-making power over their use. Special attention is given to physical accessibility of key facilities such as latrines, water points, health centers, and distribution sites, as well as challenges faced during service access.
The questions assess awareness of complaint and feedback mechanisms in cases of unequal access, and identify the most vulnerable groups in the community along with the underlying causes of their vulnerability.
Furthermore, the guide explores the priority needs of women, their participation in community activities, and the extent of their roles and influence in decision-making processes. It evaluates their representation within community leadership structures and gathers suggestions for improving their inclusion and advocacy.
Barriers preventing women from expressing their concerns are highlighted, alongside potential mechanisms to enhance their participation. The role of men and boys in supporting women’s involvement in decision-making is also examined.
Finally, the discussion addresses safety and protection concerns, including unsafe locations, risks faced by women, emergency preparedness, and access to support systems. It also gathers recommendations for creating a safer, more inclusive, and enabling environment for women in the community.

The safety audit conducted at Tabaria alKhair site in Khan Younis identified serious protection, environmental, and infrastructure concerns affecting displaced families, particularly women and girls. The site hosts approximately 5,464 residents and experiences severe overcrowding . Tents are placed very close together, resulting in limited privacy and insufficient movement space for residents within the site.
The complete absence of night lighting creates major safety and protection risks, especially for women, children, and older persons. Poor visibility during nighttime movement has led to multiple accidents, including children falling into open pits.
Water access remains inadequate, with serious shortages affecting daily use. Although a water line exists within the site, supply is limited to once or twice per week, leading to tensions and disputes among displaced people during water distribution. Sanitation facilities are available but remain insufficient in terms of privacy and dignity, as multiple families are forced to share the same latrine facilities. In addition, there is no dedicated safe space for women, and the site management room is temporarily being used for women’s activities and awareness sessions.
The presence of open pits throughout the site poses severe safety hazards, particularly for children and older persons. A previous fatal incident involving a child falling into a pit was reported at the site. Waste accumulation is another major concern, contributing to foul odors, rodents, and deteriorating public health conditions, while residents continue to request improved waste removal mechanisms.
Seasonal flooding significantly affects the site due to differences in ground elevation and poor drainage. Rainwater accumulates in lower areas, flooding tents and damaging wooden structures within the site. The spread of stray dogs and insects, combined with the absence of proper site boundaries, has also contributed to increasing health risks, including skin diseases. The assessment highlights urgent needs for improved lighting, safer pathways, drainage interventions, sandbags, waste management systems, dedicated women’s spaces, safer sanitation facilities, and enhanced protection measures for vulnerable groups within the site.

The safety audit conducted at Sanad Site in Gaza identified serious protection, environmental, and infrastructure concerns affecting displaced families, particularly women and girls. The site hosts approximately 747 residents and suffers from overcrowding, with tents placed extremely close together, resulting in limited privacy and narrow pathways that restrict safe movement within the site. 
The absence of night lighting creates major protection and safety risks, including increased theft concerns and multiple injuries caused by falls in poorly visible pathways. Elderly people and children are particularly vulnerable, and incidents related to nighttime movement have already been reported. 
Water and sanitation conditions are critically inadequate. Water availability is extremely limited, as the site well operates for only a short period daily due to dependence on an external generator. Drinking water is often used for domestic purposes because of severe shortages, and no regular organization currently provides sufficient domestic water support. Latrines are in extremely poor condition and are unsuitable for human use, with several families sharing each facility. Privacy and hygiene standards are severely lacking, creating serious public health concerns. In addition, there is no dedicated safe space for women, although educational activities and awareness sessions are conducted in the learning school within the site. 
The site contains a very large number of open pits, which site management identified as a major threat to children and residents due to the risk of falls and injuries. Solid waste accumulation is also widespread throughout the site, contributing to the spread of diseases, foul odors, rodents, and skin infections, while waste removal capacity remains insufficient. 
Seasonal flooding further worsens living conditions, as rainwater floods tents, fills pathways, and causes soil erosion between elevated and low-lying areas. Residents also face risks from slipping and movement accidents during heavy rainfall. Additional concerns include the widespread presence of rodents and reptiles due to the site’s proximity to a waste dump. The assessment highlights urgent needs for improved lighting, water supply, sanitation rehabilitation, drainage systems, waste management, safer movement pathways, pit rehabilitation, and enhanced protection measures for women, children, and vulnerable groups within the site.

The safety audit conducted at AlKareem (Abu Khadra) site in Gaza identified serious protection, environmental, and infrastructure concerns affecting displaced families, particularly women and girls. The site hosts approximately 1,190 residents and suffers from overcrowding, with narrow pathways and almost no privacy between shelters, as tents are separated only by tarpaulin sheets. 
The absence of night lighting creates major safety and protection risks throughout the site. Poor visibility has increased incidents of theft, the spread of rodents, and the presence of stray animals. Several injuries related to nighttime movement have also been reported, including a serious fracture suffered by the site manager. 
Water and sanitation conditions remain critically inadequate. The site currently lacks proper water distribution points, although efforts are underway to extend a water network through humanitarian support. Existing latrines are shared among multiple families and are in very poor condition, lacking sufficient water supply and producing foul odors that create serious public health concerns. Site management highlighted the urgent need for proper sanitation facilities to reduce disease risks among residents. In addition, there is no dedicated safe space for women, with the learning school currently being used temporarily for awareness and educational activities. 
The site contains approximately 140 open pits, many of which remain uncovered despite repeated requests for intervention. These pits pose severe risks to children and residents, and previous incidents involving children falling into pits have already occurred. Waste management is another major concern, as the absence of waste containers has led to widespread waste accumulation, foul odors, and increased disease risks within the site. 
Seasonal flooding significantly affects the site because it is located at a lower elevation than surrounding streets, causing rainwater runoff and soil erosion that threaten tents and resident safety. Additional concerns include the spread of rodents, reptiles, skin diseases, stray dogs, and security risks related to nearby gunfire incidents. The assessment highlights urgent needs for improved lighting, water supply systems, sanitation rehabilitation, pit covering, drainage works, waste management, safer movement pathways, and enhanced protection measures for women, children, and other vulnerable groups within the site.

The safety audit conducted at AlJundi AlMajhoul site in Gaza identified severe protection, environmental, and infrastructure concerns affecting displaced families, particularly women and girls. The site hosts approximately 757 residents and experiences significant overcrowding, with around 140 tents located within a limited area of approximately 10 dunums. Narrow pathways and the close proximity of shelters have resulted in a complete lack of privacy and restricted safe movement within the site. 
The absence of night lighting presents major protection and safety risks. Poor visibility has contributed to increased security incident , numerous injuries among children and older persons, and incidents involving women and children falling into open pits. The lack of lighting has also contributed to the spread of rodents within the site. 
Water and sanitation conditions are critically inadequate. Residents depend on drinking water trucks and are forced to use drinking water for domestic purposes due to the absence of a regular water supply system. The site also lacks water storage tanks. Existing latrines are extremely poor in condition, enclosed only with fabric materials, and shared by several families, resulting in a complete lack of privacy and unsuitable sanitation conditions. In addition, there is no dedicated safe space for women, with the learning school temporarily being used for awareness and educational sessions. 
The presence of open pits throughout the site poses severe safety risks, particularly for children. Serious incidents have already occurred, including a child falling into a pit and requiring intensive medical care. Site residents lack the resources necessary to safely cover these pits. Waste management services are also insufficient, as waste accumulates inside the site between municipal collection periods, contributing to the spread of diseases and skin infections. 
Seasonal flooding represents another major challenge, as the site was heavily flooded during recent storms due to uneven ground and the lack of drainage systems. Additional concerns include rodent infestations, reported biting incidents, and attacks by stray dogs on residents. The assessment highlights urgent needs for improved lighting, drainage systems, safer sanitation facilities, waste management, pit rehabilitation, safer pathways, and enhanced protection measures for women, children, and vulnerable groups within the site.

At Al-Fedaa site, all 23 men, including 3 elderly, described a major shift from previously stable livelihoods to almost complete dependence on humanitarian aid. Men are mainly occupied with survival tasks such as securing food and water, facing high stress and limited income opportunities. Access to services is difficult due to overcrowding, long distances, and poor infrastructure, with persons with disabilities facing greater barriers. Living conditions are unsafe, with multiple environmental and protection risks. Participation in community roles is very limited, and decision-making remains centralized. Key needs include financial assistance, psychosocial support, improved infrastructure, safer conditions, and more inclusive engagement opportunities.

At Al-Shaheed Jameel site, all 12 participants, including 3 elderly, described a sharp decline from pre-crisis livelihoods to conditions focused entirely on survival. Persons with disabilities are fully excluded from employment and rely heavily on family and community support for daily needs. Access to services is extremely limited due to poor infrastructure and lack of accessibility, with significant inequality in resource distribution. Living conditions are inadequate, contributing to stress, social tensions, and insecurity. Participation in community roles is absent, and decision-making is centralized. Key needs include accessible facilities, financial assistance, psychosocial support, improved services, and stronger community engagement and communication mechanisms.

At Al-Jawhari site, all 13 participants, including 3 elderly, described a sharp decline from previously stable livelihoods to severe economic hardship and near-total dependence on humanitarian assistance. Men are largely unable to secure stable income and spend most of their time meeting basic survival needs, while persons with disabilities face heightened exclusion and dependency on others. Access to food, water, and essential services is inconsistent and constrained by long distances, overcrowding, and lack of accessible infrastructure. Living conditions are unsafe, with risks related to poor hygiene, disease spread, and inadequate facilities. Participation in community roles is absent, and decision-making remains centralized. Key priorities include financial support, accessible services, improved infrastructure, psychosocial support, and more inclusive engagement mechanisms.

Topic: Site Management Committee Establishment, Coordination or Planning
Summary: A coordination meeting was held at Al-Jawhari site with representatives of blocks and Acted SM team, aiming to organize fieldwork and enhance coordination. The meeting came in light of proactive field initiatives carried out by some committees, which required clarifying the governing organizational framework. Discussions focused on the importance of a clear organizational structure, defining roles, and improving communication mechanisms, in addition to adhering to the Memorandum of Understanding and the Code of Conduct. Emphasis was also placed on clear institutional representation and avoiding overlaps in responsibilities. It was agreed to form a committee composed of block representatives under the name “Monitoring Committee.”

At Al-Jawhari site, two women’s sessions (15 and 40 participants, including 1 and 3 elderly respectively) revealed a significant shift toward survival-based living and increased burdens on women. In the first session (15 participants), all reported no decision-making power, no active roles, and lack of safety, highlighting risks such as fear of exploitation, harassment, and ineffective complaint mechanisms. In the second session (40 participants), all confirmed increased responsibilities and reliance on community kitchens, while the majority reported unequal access to services and limited trust in feedback systems. Although participation was higher (40/40), awareness of representation structures remained low. Across both sessions, women identified children and elderly as highly vulnerable groups. Overall, findings reflect high vulnerability, limited control over resources, safety concerns, and the urgent need for improved protection, inclusive participation, better services, and empowerment opportunities.

At Al-Rimal Al-Thahabiea site, two women’s sessions (20 and 19 participants, including 2 and 5 elderly respectively) highlighted increased burdens and vulnerability among women. In the first session (20 participants), all reported significantly increased responsibilities, active participation (20/20), awareness of complaint mechanisms, and representation in site structures, yet all confirmed unequal access to resources and lack of safety due to environmental risks. In the second session (19 participants), all reported no active roles in decision-making, unequal access (19/19), and ineffective complaint systems, despite awareness of channels. Across both sessions, women and children were identified as the most vulnerable. Overall, findings show heavy workloads, limited control, safety concerns, and the need for livelihood opportunities, psychosocial support, improved protection, and stronger, more responsive community engagement mechanisms.

At Al-Shaheed Jameel site, two women’s sessions (12 and 15 participants, including 1 and 3 elderly respectively) highlighted increased burdens and vulnerability following displacement. In the first session (12 participants), all reported increased responsibilities, participation in activities (12/12), but lack of awareness of complaint mechanisms and limited involvement in decision-making. In the second session (15 participants), all confirmed increased workload and reliance on community kitchens, while most reported limited participation (11/15 not participating) and lack of access to complaint systems (15/15). Across both sessions, women and elderly were consistently identified as the most vulnerable. Overall, findings indicate high stress, unequal access, weak feedback mechanisms, and the need for improved services, protection, psychosocial support, and inclusive engagement.

Topic: Site Management Committee Establishment, Coordination or Planning
Summary:
ToR signing session: After the SM team successfully established and upgraded the committees, then SM proceeded with SMCs validation step. Consequently, the SM moved forward with preparing the ToRs for each site individually and finally coordinated and scheduling of ToRs signing sessions. 

The ToR outlined the roles and responsibilities of both the Committees and the ACTED Site Management (SM) team.
In addition, the organigram of the committee and the structural hierarchy of Site Management are provided as annexes to this document. The ToR serves as a guiding framework to enable the committees to operate effectively, ensure clarity of roles, and contribute to the overall resilience of the community. In addition, SM team signed the Code of Conduct with the committee members after reading it to them and discussing its contents. 

This step represented a significant advancement in formalizing the committees’ roles and enhancing their involvement in site management activities.

At Al-Fidaa site, two women’s sessions (16 and 15 participants, including 2 and 0 elderly respectively) highlighted significant challenges following displacement. In the first session (16 participants), all reported increased physical and environmental burdens, lack of awareness of complaint mechanisms (16/16), and unequal access to resources, despite relatively high participation (14/16). In the second session (15 participants), all confirmed increased stress, lack of privacy, and reliance on community kitchens, while most reported unequal access and mixed awareness of complaint channels. Participation was moderate (10/15), but decision-making remained externally controlled in both sessions. Across both groups, children, elderly, and persons with illnesses were identified as highly vulnerable. Overall, findings indicate high stress, limited control, weak feedback systems, and urgent needs for services, protection, and psychosocial support.

Mosab A Site, located in the Sheikh Ejleen area in Gaza, is host approximately 880 displaced persons. The site has partial lighting provided through NRC's CLP project and an external initiative, but coverage remains insufficient. Critical areas including the latrines and the Yasmeen medical point have no lighting. Women rely on mobile phone flashlights for nighttime navigation, which increases their exposure to protection risks after dark. The site is considered more organized than many others in the area, with pathways present, though these are limited in scope and do not fully ensure safe movement. Privacy within tents is inadequate.
Water availability stands at approximately 70% coverage, dependent on municipality-supported generators. Any disruption in fuel supply significantly impacts access to water. Water is delivered directly to tents, which reduces queue-related risks for domestic use, though controlled queues remain in place for drinking water collection. Eight latrines are available at the site; however, they are inaccessible to persons with disabilities and are not gender-segregated, which compromises the safety and privacy of women and girls. No shower facilities are available. Although doors have locks, the overall sanitation conditions remain inadequate. The presence of stray dogs at night near the latrines further increases risk for residents.
There is no safe space designated for women at the site. No uncovered soak pits were identified, though solid waste accumulation and flooding risks are present. Stray dogs remain a persistent protection concern throughout the site, particularly at night. The absence of proper lighting at critical service points — especially latrines and the medical point — represents the most urgent safety gap at Mosab A. The partial water supply, while better than at many other sites, remains vulnerable to fuel shortages. Priority improvements needed include expansion of lighting coverage, gender-segregated and disability-accessible sanitation facilities, waste management systems, and the establishment of a safe and secure space dedicated to women and girls.

Topic: Programming Specific Meetings (e.g. project inductions, cash for work, etc.)
Summary: This meeting focused on introducing the concept of Community-Led Initiatives (CLI) and explaining how ACTED’s Site Management team supports them. The safety audit conducted at Al Haya Zawaida site in Zawaida area identified several critical protection, safety, and infrastructure concerns affecting displaced populations, particularly women and girls. The site hosts approximately 975 residents and, while generally organized with adequate spacing and privacy between shelters, significant gaps remain in essential services and safety measures.
The absence of night lighting across the site poses serious protection and safety risks. Several injuries have already occurred due to poor visibility, including falls into open pits and fractures during nighttime movement. In addition, the site contains numerous open pits, many of which remain uncovered or inadequately protected, creating further hazards for residents.
Water, sanitation, and hygiene conditions remain inadequate. There is no reliable domestic water source, and drinking water depends on irregular tanker deliveries from humanitarian organizations. Although latrines exist, many are privately constructed and lack minimum safety and hygiene standards, with insufficient facilities and inconsistent suitability for use. No dedicated safe space for women and girls is available within the site.
Environmental and seasonal risks are also significant. The site’s clay soil becomes heavily flooded during winter, restricting movement and access to services, markets, and clinics while increasing the likelihood of slips, injuries, and tent flooding. The site is unfenced and exposed, contributing to protection concerns such as theft and risks from stray animals. Waste management support is currently temporary and may cease soon, potentially increasing environmental health concerns.
Additional concerns highlighted during the assessment include high fire risks, with previous incidents resulting in injuries and loss of shelters and personal belongings. As summer approaches, residents may also face increased risks related to insects, rodents, reptiles, snakes, and disease transmission. Overall, the audit indicates an urgent need for site improvement interventions focused on lighting, drainage, safe pit covering, WASH infrastructure, fencing, fire mitigation measures, and enhanced protection services for women and vulnerable groups.

Falastine Site in Tell Al-Hawa, Gaza, houses approximately 750 displaced persons and presents multiple critical safety concerns across all assessed dimensions. The site has no night lighting, which has enabled stray dogs to roam freely, attacking women and elderly residents who attempt to use latrines after dark. The absence of physical boundaries around the site compounds this problem significantly. The site is severely overcrowded, with tents positioned extremely close together, narrow pathways, and a complete absence of privacy for residents. These conditions create daily movement hazards and reduce dignity for all displaced people, especially women and girls.
Water access is critically inadequate. There are no dedicated water distribution points within the site, and residents rely on a single municipal water line that supplies water only two days per week for two hours each session. This scarcity has triggered frequent disputes among displaced persons whenever water becomes available. Sanitation conditions are similarly alarming — while each tent has a private latrine, these consist entirely of uncovered soak pits that are unhygienic and pose a serious fall risk to children. None of the latrines meet minimum standards of safety or functionality.
There is no dedicated safe space for women at the site, though site management has formally requested the urgent provision of such a space. Regarding site improvement, approximately 120 soak pits are distributed throughout the site, many uncovered, presenting constant fall hazards. Solid waste accumulates inside the site without municipal collection, generating foul odors, attracting rodents, and contributing to the spread of infectious diseases and skin conditions. Site management has requested waste containers and workers to transport waste out of the site.
Flooding presents a seasonal risk, as the entire site was completely inundated during recent storms due to uneven terrain and the absence of any drainage infrastructure. Additional safety barriers include increasing rates of theft and the ongoing threat from uncontrolled stray dogs, both of which threaten the personal security and wellbeing of displaced residents. In summary, Falastin Site requires urgent intervention across nearly all categories: lighting, water supply, sanitation, solid waste management, drainage, physical security, and the provision of dedicated safe spaces for women and girls."

The safety audit conducted at Al Tareni site in Zawaida area identified several safety, protection, and infrastructure concerns affecting displaced families, particularly women and girls. The site hosts approximately 641 residents and is not currently overcrowded due to its relatively large area. Shelters are mainly composed of tarpaulin and ready-made fabric tents.
One of the most critical concerns is the complete absence of night lighting throughout the site. This has resulted in multiple injuries and serious accidents, including fractures caused by falls while moving at night. The lack of lighting significantly increases protection and mobility risks for residents, especially women, children, and older persons.
Water and sanitation conditions remain inadequate. A temporary water source supported by a humanitarian organization is available; however, it is only guaranteed for a limited period. Most latrines do not meet minimum sanitation standards and pose health and hygiene risks to residents. Although the site includes a dedicated and separate safe space for women, additional protection measures are still required.
The assessment also highlighted the presence of many open pits across the site, creating safety hazards and restricting safe movement for residents. Seasonal flooding remains another major challenge, as the clay soil accumulates rainwater and contributes to soil erosion and damage to tents during winter. Residents have attempted to create simple drainage channels to reduce flooding impacts, but risks remain high.
Environmental and health concerns were also observed, including risks from rodents, reptiles, and snakes due to dense vegetation surrounding the site. Incidents involving children being bitten by reptiles have already been reported. Fire hazards inside tents caused by cooking and heating activities further increase the vulnerability of displaced families. In addition, many households face severe economic hardship, with limited or no income sources, highlighting the need for livelihood support and cash-for-work opportunities.

The urgency for expanded lighting — particularly at latrines and medical points — cannot be overstated. Mosab B requires immediate investment in gender-segregated sanitation facilities accessible to persons with disabilities, improved lighting coverage across the entire site, solid waste collection services, and a dedicated women's safe space to address the significant protection vulnerabilities facing the displaced population.

The safety audit conducted at Fares site in Gaza identified significant protection, environmental, and infrastructure risks affecting displaced families, particularly women and girls. The site hosts approximately 1,150 residents and, although not severely overcrowded, the large accumulation of rubble from destroyed buildings has reduced usable living space and created hazardous conditions throughout the site.
One of the most critical concerns is the complete absence of night lighting. Several injuries have been reported due to falls and movement accidents at night, including serious injuries suffered by women and children. The uneven terrain and widespread building debris, including exposed concrete and iron rods, further increase movement risks and obstruct safe access within the site.
Water and sanitation conditions remain inadequate. The site suffers from severe water shortages, with no reliable domestic water source available. Drinking water is delivered irregularly by humanitarian organizations, while existing water tanks remain unusable due to the lack of a water supply system. Most latrines fail to meet minimum hygiene, privacy, and safety standards, and the available public latrines are in poor condition and vulnerable to deterioration. In addition, there is no dedicated safe space for women, as existing activity tents are shared and do not provide secure or private facilities for women and girls.
Although most pits within the site are currently covered, concerns remain regarding future overflow and associated health and safety risks. Seasonal flooding is another major issue, as rainwater accumulates in low-lying areas due to the clay soil, damaging tents and limiting residents’ movement during winter.
Additional safety concerns include the spread of rodents and reptiles caused by the accumulation of rubble and debris, as well as the presence of stray animals entering the site. Fire hazards are also significant due to the use of open fires for cooking and heating, with previous incidents already causing damage to shelters and family belongings. Overall, the assessment highlights urgent needs for lighting installation, rubble removal, site leveling, improved WASH facilities, drainage solutions, safer movement pathways, and enhanced protection measures for women and vulnerable groups.

"Qasr Al-Mina, located along the Gaza coastline, shelters approximately 970 displaced persons across 170 families within a 7-dunum site. The safety audit reveals serious deficiencies across all key indicators. The site has no night lighting, which severely impacts the safety and mobility of residents, particularly women, children, and the elderly. Poor visibility has led to increased activity of stray dogs and rodents, frequent trips and falls along unlit pathways, and stumbling caused by unsecured tent pegs. These conditions have created a persistently hazardous nighttime environment.
The site is heavily overcrowded, with tents attached closely to one another, complete absence of privacy, and narrow pathways. This extreme density has generated tensions among displaced families and significantly compromises the physical safety and psychological wellbeing of residents. Water supply is wholly inadequate — the only source is water trucks provided through IBRF. The site's coastal location results in highly saline groundwater, forcing residents to use their limited drinking water allocation for domestic purposes, rapidly depleting this scarce resource.
Latrine conditions at the site are critical. One latrine is shared among every four families, facilities are mostly soak pits emitting strong foul odors, and hygiene conditions are extremely poor. The latrines contribute to the spread of skin infections, diseases, and epidemics. There is no dedicated safe space for women; they currently use the site management room for sessions and workshops, which is not an appropriate substitute.
While there are no uncovered latrine pits specifically, an open municipal sewage and drainage channel exists within the site without any cover, posing both safety and health risks. Solid waste accumulates at the edges of the site, previously collected by municipal trucks but no longer serviced for an extended period. Management has requested provision of waste containers. The uneven terrain of the site makes it prone to flooding during winter, with rainwater flowing directly into tents and damaging residents' belongings. Stray dogs and rodents compound the risk of disease transmission throughout the site. Immediate multi-sectoral intervention is needed to address water, sanitation, lighting, flooding, and waste management."

Al-Amal Site, located in Al-Mawassi northwest of Khan Younis, accommodates approximately 1,700 displaced persons. While the site benefits from partial lighting infrastructure installed through NRC's CLP project, this lighting is considered insufficient for safe nighttime mobility. Multiple critical areas remain unlit, including the latrines and the medical point. Women lack access to handheld flashlights, limiting their movement after dark. Multiple incidents of falls among elderly people, women, and children have been documented, and insufficient lighting has contributed to increased theft within the site.
The site is severely overcrowded, with no clearly defined pathways and no locks or partitions between tents to ensure privacy. Approximately 30 tents are hosting multiple families, intensifying congestion and protection risks. Water supply is critically inadequate — due to the municipality's failure to provide water and ongoing diesel shortages for well operation, water tanks are refilled only once every nine days, far below the needs of the displaced population. Congestion at water collection points creates additional safety hazards for women and persons with disabilities.
The latrine situation is mixed. Three public latrines near the prayer area serve general use but are frequently overcrowded and lack sufficient cleaning materials. The remaining latrines are private and located inside family tents, are basic pit latrines without gender segregation, and generate hygiene risks including strong odors and the danger of children falling into pits. There is no functioning safe space for women at the site. Open pits and solid waste accumulation present ongoing environmental and physical hazards throughout the site.
The site is prone to winter flooding, further exacerbating the risks posed by open pits and poor drainage. Theft is reported as an increasing concern, and the presence of stray dogs adds to safety risks, particularly at night. The combination of overcrowding, water scarcity, inadequate sanitation, and insufficient lighting makes Al-Amal Site one of the more vulnerable sites in the assessed area. Priority interventions should focus on expanding water access, improving latrine infrastructure, enhancing lighting coverage, and establishing a dedicated safe space for women and girls."

FGD  – Men and Persons with Disabilities (PwDs)
The discussion guide explores the roles, experiences, and challenges faced by men and persons with disabilities (PwDs) in the community, both before and during the current crisis. It examines changes in daily responsibilities, levels of independence, and reliance on others for basic activities.
It also focuses on access to food, non-food items, and essential services, including how these resources are distributed, controlled, and whether access is equitable. Particular attention is given to barriers faced by PwDs in accessing facilities such as water points, latrines, health centers, and distribution sites.

The safety audit conducted at AlEkhwa site in Zawaida area identified several protection, safety, and environmental concerns affecting displaced families, particularly women and girls. The site hosts approximately 413 residents and experiences varying levels of overcrowding, with some sections suffering from congestion, limited privacy, and closely spaced tents. While pathways exist, they remain unpaved and uneven, limiting safe movement within the site.
Although lighting support has been provided, night lighting remains insufficient across the site. Existing lighting units do not adequately cover pathways and open spaces, and the operating duration is limited, increasing safety risks during nighttime movement.
Water and sanitation conditions are inadequate. There is no domestic water source inside the site, and residents depend on transported water deliveries from humanitarian organizations. Women and girls face significant burdens carrying water over long distances and are exposed to harassment, violence, and overcrowding during water collection. Most latrines are privately constructed and fail to meet minimum hygiene, accessibility, privacy, and protection standards. There are no designated bathing areas, and bathing takes place inside the same latrines, which are constructed from tarpaulin and fabric materials that do not ensure privacy. The existing women’s tent also does not provide sufficient privacy or protection.
The assessment further identified the presence of open pits covered only with basic metal sheets, creating serious safety and health hazards for residents. Waste management is also a major concern, as informal dumping areas around the site contribute to the spread of insects, diseases, and environmental health risks. Seasonal flooding affects low-lying areas within the site, causing rainwater accumulation and damage to tents due to soil erosion.
Additional concerns include the site being open and unfenced, increasing risks related to theft and insecurity. Fire hazards, rodents, reptiles, and the spread of diseases also pose significant threats to residents, especially during summer months. The assessment highlights urgent needs for improved lighting, fencing, safer WASH infrastructure, proper waste management, drainage improvements, and site maintenance activities, alongside livelihood and cash-for-work opportunities to support vulnerable households.

Seasonal flooding significantly affects the site, as low-lying areas accumulate rainwater, causing erosion, tent damage, and restricted access to and from the site. Flooding has also damaged personal belongings and disrupted movement for residents. Additional concerns include theft risks, attacks by stray animals, fire incidents, and increasing threats from insects, rodents, and reptiles. The assessment highlights urgent needs for improved lighting, drainage systems, waste management, safer sanitation infrastructure, site leveling, fencing, and enhanced protection measures for women and vulnerable groups, alongside cash-for-work opportunities to support site maintenance and cleaning activities.

The safety audit conducted at AlArd AlTaiba site in Khan Younis identified several protection, environmental, and infrastructure concerns affecting displaced families, particularly women and girls. The site hosts approximately 3,584 residents. Seasonal flooding also affects the site, particularly in low-lying areas where rainwater accumulates and damages tents. Families living in elevated sections face additional mobility restrictions during rainy periods. Other concerns include fire risks, stray animals, rodents, reptiles, and the spread of insects and diseases, especially during summer months. The assessment highlights urgent needs for improved lighting, drainage systems, sewage management, safer sanitation facilities, pit rehabilitation, waste management, land leveling, tent maintenance, and enhanced protection measures for women and vulnerable groups, alongside cash-for-work opportunities to support site improvement activities.

Al-Sheikh Ejleen A Site, located in Tell Al-Hawa, Gaza, accommodates approximately 1,249 displaced persons across 400 households. The site has no night lighting, which has directly contributed to serious protection incidents: women have been harassed, tents attacked, and thefts committed under cover of darkness. The absence of lighting is the most critical safety gap at this site. Unlike many other assessed sites, Al-Sheikh Ejleen A is not classified as overcrowded — the site is large, though somewhat unorganized and scattered in layout. The spaciousness provides residents with some degree of privacy within tents and allows for wider pathways, which is a relative advantage.
Water supply reaches approximately 50% of the population. Distribution is managed by responsible committees, and the fact that most residents are relatives of one another reduces interpersonal conflicts at water collection points. However, half the population still lacks consistent water access. Latrine conditions are inadequate; no specific details were documented in the audit, but the classification indicates non-functioning facilities. There is no safe space for women at the site.
Open pits present a significant physical hazard — each tent has an associated pit, many positioned along pathways and between tents. Five incidents of residents falling into these pits have already been recorded. Solid waste accumulation presents environmental and pest-related health risks. Flooding risks are present during winter months. The combination of no lighting, documented protection incidents against women, and multiple physical hazards from open pits makes Al-Sheikh Ejleen A a high-priority site for safety intervention. While the relatively lower density is an advantage, it does not mitigate the urgent need for lighting infrastructure, proper pit covers, latrine rehabilitation, solid waste management, and the establishment of a safe and secure space specifically for women and girls. Security measures to prevent theft and harassment must also be addressed as an immediate priority.

Night lighting is entirely absent, a condition that has directly enabled serious protection incidents: women have been harassed, tents attacked, and thefts have occurred at night. The lack of any lighting infrastructure represents the most acute safety concern at the site. Similar to Al-Sheikh Ejleen B is not classified as overcrowded. Its large, scattered layout provides residents with relatively more privacy within their tents and wider pathways than densely packed sites, which is a positive comparative factor.

The familial relationships among most residents reduce queue-related tensions at water distribution points. However, half of the population still lacks reliable water access. Al-Horia Site in Khan Younis, located at Al Mawasi hosts approximately 1,660 displaced persons across 456 households. The site has lighting infrastructure, but the existing floodlights are old and extensively damaged by storms and wind, rendering them largely ineffective. There is an urgent need for functional lighting along pathways, near latrines, and at water points. The current darkness prevents women and persons with disabilities from moving safely after dark, exposes children to falls and trips over tent stakes, and poses a direct risk to life and personal safety.
The site is overcrowded, with limited pathways and no privacy within shelters. Several shelters host multiple families, increasing the risk of disease transmission and negatively affecting residents' mental health and overall safety. Water access is partially available, with existing water points insufficient to meet demand, causing long queues. Additional water points are urgently required to ensure equitable access. Latrines exist but require significant maintenance: existing wells need cleaning and pumping, and new wells need to be opened. Cash-for-work staff are specifically requested to carry out this maintenance work.
There is no safe space for women at the site. Seventeen open pits have been identified, presenting environmental and health risks including the spread of disease, emission of foul odors, and fall hazards. Solid waste accumulates throughout the site, contributing to rodent infestation and disease risk. Flooding is a seasonal concern. The combination of storm-damaged lighting infrastructure, overcrowding, inadequate water points, deteriorating latrines, and multiple open pits creates a compounded risk environment for this large displaced population. Priority interventions include urgent replacement and expansion of lighting infrastructure, construction of additional water points, well cleaning and rehabilitation through cash-for-work programming, pit coverage, solid waste management systems, and provision of a safe space for women and girls.

Al-Fajr Site, located in Al-Mawassi, Khan Younis, hosts approximately 1,230 displaced persons across a population recorded as 1,250 households. The site has partial lighting, but coverage is insufficient with no lighting near latrines or water points. The risk of injury from tent stakes and open pits is elevated, particularly for children, women, the elderly, and persons with disabilities who require safe and accessible movement at night. The site is severely overcrowded with very narrow pathways, limiting safe movement throughout the settlement. Privacy is entirely absent for residents.
Water points exist at the site but are classified as insufficient for the population's needs. Additional tanks and jerry cans are required. Serious concerns were noted at water collection points, including harassment of women in queues, inaccessibility for persons with disabilities, and dangerously long waiting times that create both safety and protection risks. Latrine infrastructure comprises approximately 140 communal latrines, which, while nominally large in number, remain inadequate for the size of the population. These latrines suffer from chronic overcrowding, very poor hygiene conditions, strong foul odors, and a lack of proper gender separation, raising significant protection concerns for women and girls. The current situation contributes to environmental contamination and an elevated risk of disease transmission throughout the site.
No dedicated safe space for women exists. No open pits were identified as a current hazard. Solid waste accumulation and seasonal flooding remain concerns. The harassment of women at water points reflects a deeper protection gap that requires both structural and behavioral responses. In summary, Al-Fajr Site faces serious challenges around WASH adequacy, women's safety in public spaces, lighting coverage, and privacy. Recommended priority actions include expanding water point infrastructure, addressing harassment through community and protection mechanisms, improving latrine capacity and gender segregation, extending lighting to latrines and water areas, and establishing a safe and protected space for women and girls at the site.

Al-Hamd Site, located in Al-Mawassi in Khan Younis accommodates approximately 1,074 displaced persons across 651 households on a 100-dunum plot. The site has no night lighting, creating conditions that particularly endanger women — who face elevated harassment risks after dark — as well as children who may become lost, and the broader population whose access to services is severely limited at night. The site is overcrowded with no clearly defined pathways, and multiple families share single tents with no privacy. Children move unsafely throughout the settlement, and the large area without any organization compounds these movement risks.
Water conditions are critically severe. Coverage stands at approximately only 5% of the population's needs, making Al-Hamd one of the most water-deprived sites in the assessed area. Long queues cause particular hardship for women and persons with disabilities. Skin diseases have been documented and attributed directly to the water shortage. Latrine facilities are classified as inadequate with no further details available in the audit record.
There is no safe space for women at the site. One hundred soak pits are distributed throughout the site, representing a severe and constant fall hazard for all residents, particularly children. Stagnant water in these pits produces strong odors and provides breeding grounds for rodents and disease vectors. Solid waste accumulation compounds the environmental health burden, and flooding during winter months adds further risk. The extreme water scarcity at Al-Hamd Site — covering less than one-twentieth of actual needs — combined with the total absence of lighting, 100 open soak pits, overcrowding without pathways, and skin disease outbreaks, makes this one of the highest-priority sites for urgent and comprehensive intervention. Immediate actions should include emergency water provision, pit coverage, lighting installation, latrine rehabilitation, pathway establishment, solid waste management, and establishment of a women's safe space.

Al-Masmiya Site, located in Deir Al-Balah, houses approximately 892 displaced persons . The site has lighting provided along main pathways by NRC, but coverage is assessed as insufficient. Significant risks persist due to unlit areas where residents — particularly women and children — are at risk of falling into open pits, tripping on tent pegs, and slipping on clay soil that becomes especially hazardous in the dark. Theft is reported as an ongoing problem. Children have wandered into the wrong tents due to poor visibility, and many displaced persons are unable to move after sunset. The site is overcrowded despite being relatively organized in layout. There are no pathways between tents, and privacy is lacking, with multiple families sharing tents.
Water access is critically inadequate. A single water line from a desalination station serves the entire site without a fixed schedule, and the line is located approximately one kilometer away on the public road. This distance makes water collection impossible for women, children, and persons with disabilities without assistance. Queue-related problems have been reported. Latrines are private but shared among every five families, creating persistent conflicts, privacy deficits, and queue management difficulties. Facilities are very basic and below minimum standards.
No safe space for women is available at the site. One hundred and fifty open pits have been identified, representing an extremely serious fall hazard for all residents. Solid waste accumulation contributes to pest infestation and disease spread. Seasonal flooding is a risk. The clay soil composition of the site adds a unique hazard in wet conditions, increasing slipping risks for all residents. Al-Masmiya Site requires urgent interventions including extended lighting coverage, emergency water access solutions closer to the site, latrine rehabilitation and privacy improvements, systematic pit covering, solid waste management, and provision of a safe space for women. Accessibility improvements for persons with disabilities and women at water points are also a critical priority.

"Al-Ramleh Site, located in Deir Al-Balah, hosts approximately 776 displaced persons. The site has external lighting that covers water collection points, but internal and pathway lighting is absent, making nighttime movement throughout the site hazardous. The site is situated on a cliff with rough and uneven terrain, which creates extremely dangerous movement conditions for residents. The site manager sustained a serious injury — breaking both legs — while descending the cliff, illustrating the severity of the terrain hazard. Despite this, residents must navigate these conditions daily.
The site is overcrowded, with no privacy available for residents, though pathways do exist. Water access is critically inadequate: only two water collection points exist, both positioned at the cliff edge. This dangerous location has caused falls during water collection. Women — particularly widows and divorcees — and persons with disabilities are effectively unable to collect water independently, creating a severe access inequality. Latrine conditions are very basic with no privacy, well below acceptable minimum standards for displaced populations.
There is no safe space for women at the site. Twenty open pits are present within the site, and while some pits belonging to other families are covered, improper covering means children remain exposed to fall risks. Solid waste accumulation represents both an environmental and health hazard. Seasonal flooding is a concern given the cliff terrain. The geographic setting of Al-Ramleh Site on a cliff represents a uniquely compound risk — it simultaneously endangers water access, restricts mobility, and worsens flooding and drainage challenges. The inaccessibility of water points for women and persons with disabilities is a particularly critical protection gap. Priority recommendations include: relocating or adding safer water collection points, installing comprehensive internal pathway lighting, rehabilitating latrine infrastructure, securing all open pits, establishing a women's safe space, and implementing emergency flooding mitigation measures appropriate for the cliff terrain."

Al-Tawoun Site, located in Al-Daraj near the Yarmouk Popular Market in Gaza, is among the largest assessed sites, sheltering approximately 3,118 displaced persons across 830 families on approximately 60 dunums. The site has an NRC-funded lighting system, but given the site's large size, coverage is wholly insufficient. Theft incidents and exposed soak pits have been observed. Most critically, a fire occurred at the site two months prior to the audit, resulting in the deaths of two people, injuries to 10 others, and destruction of 10 tents — an incident partly attributed to the lack of adequate lighting and emergency response capacity.
The site is highly congested and lacks privacy throughout. Overcrowding has been significantly observed across the settlement. Water supply is entirely inadequate: no water containers exist within the site. Residents rely on 10 cups per person per day from Action Against Hunger and occasional water trucks from local initiatives — quantities far below minimum standards. The municipal water line operates twice per week for 8-10 hours, primarily during nighttime hours, forcing residents to divert drinking water for domestic use and creating a dangerous cycle of water insecurity.
Latrine infrastructure is deeply inadequate for the population size. Thirty public latrines are designated for specific family groups, while private latrines are rudimentary pits covered with worn-out metal sheets and fabric. Facilities are in poor condition, lacking both privacy and hygiene. Urgent maintenance is needed throughout. No safe space for women exists at the site. Exposed soak pits and solid waste accumulation present ongoing hazards. Winter flooding risks are present. The fire incident at Al-Tawoun Site is a stark indicator of the life-threatening risks posed by insufficient lighting and emergency infrastructure at such a densely populated site. Immediate priorities include enhanced lighting coverage, expanded water access, latrine rehabilitation, fire safety measures, solid waste management, flood mitigation, and provision of a dedicated safe space for women and girls.

Al-Ameer Site, located west of Al-Quds Hospital in Gaza, accommodates approximately 1,320 displaced persons across 170 households on a 12-dunum plot. Unlike many other assessed sites, Al-Ameer is not classified as overcrowded — the site provides approximately 70 square meters per household, offering a comparatively reasonable level of comfort and privacy. However, this relative spatial advantage is overshadowed by several serious safety deficiencies.
The site has no night lighting, which creates multiple overlapping hazards. The absence of lighting significantly increases the risk of residents — especially women, children, and the elderly — falling into soak pits or tripping on the uneven ground. Rodents actively spread into tents at night in the absence of lighting, increasing disease exposure. Disorganized tent pegs and ropes throughout the site create additional tripping hazards. The collective effect of these nighttime hazards means residents are effectively confined to their tents after dark.
Water access is critically insufficient. Residents rely on a water truck that delivers approximately 5 cups twice per week, supplemented by municipal water for domestic use, available twice weekly for a maximum of two hours per session. These quantities are severely inadequate for daily household needs, and residents face a persistent and serious domestic water shortage. Latrine conditions are very poor: each household has a private latrine constructed with basic materials and a pit system covered by metal sheets and worn-out fabric. Twenty soak pits have overflowed, spreading waste in the surrounding area and significantly increasing the risk of infectious disease and epidemics.
No safe space for women exists at the site. Solid waste accumulation and winter flooding risks are present. Despite its relatively less crowded conditions, Al-Ameer Site requires urgent intervention in lighting, water supply, latrine rehabilitation, soak pit remediation, rodent control, and waste management. The 20 overflowing soak pits represent an immediate disease outbreak risk that demands immediate response.

Summary: Furniture Distribution (2 Tables, 2 Mats and 9 Chairs per site ) for SMC Activity was implemented to address the lack of proper furniture inside administrative tents across IDP sites, which was affecting communication, coordination, and service delivery. On 7 April 2026, NRC Site Management teams distributed essential furniture to 30 sites across Gaza, the Middle Area, and Khan Younis, including this site. The activity created more organized and dignified spaces for receiving displaced families and conducting daily operations. It also improved complaint handling, referrals, and communication between site management teams and IDPs. In addition, the furnished tents enhanced coordination meetings with community committees and humanitarian partners. Overall, the intervention strengthened service delivery and benefited more than 131,000 displaced individuals across the targeted sites

Topic(s): Communal Space Upgrades, Communal Space Upgrades
Summary: Care and Maintenance Tools Distribution Activity was implemented across 30 IDP sites including this site to address the lack of proper tools required for Cash for works and daily site maintenance, especially in flood-prone areas. The sites were facing challenges in digging drainage channels, removing debris, and maintaining safe pathways during rainy conditions, and also during cleaning the pathways in the site . To mitigate these issues, NRC distributed essential tools including shovels, hoes, pickaxes, wheelbarrows, plastic garden combs, and complete toolboxes. These tools enabled site teams and community workers to carry out regular cleaning, soil excavation, and drainage channel construction more effectively. The intervention also improved preparedness for flooding risks and supported safer and more organized site conditions. Overall, the activity strengthened site maintenance capacity and contributed to improving the living environment for IDPs across the targeted sites.

The Site Improvement Plan for DEB4928 – Al-Sika 1, prepared by Beit Lahia Development Association (BLDA) on 10 May 2026, identifies several environmental and infrastructure-related challenges within the displacement site.

The first issue relates to water accumulation in a low-lying area within the site due to poor ground leveling and inadequate drainage, causing movement difficulties and negatively affecting health and environmental conditions inside the site. The proposed intervention includes sand spreading and ground leveling activities to improve drainage, reduce water accumulation, and enhance accessibility within the site.

The second issue concerns the presence of randomly accumulated debris and rubble located close to tents, which contributes to the spread of rodents and insects and negatively impacts public health and safety. The proposed activities include debris removal, cleaning, and ground leveling works to improve the overall site environment and reduce health risks.

These interventions are expected to be implemented during May 2026, with each activity estimated to require approximately one working day.

The Site Improvement Plan for Mawasi Khan Younis - Al Shaheed Jameel Site highlights severe WASH, shelter, environmental, and safety challenges affecting displaced families. The site suffers from unsafe open latrines, lack of sewage systems, insufficient access to drinking and domestic water, unmanaged solid waste, flooding risks, and widespread pollution. Shelter conditions are critical due to overcrowding, poor-quality tents, lack of privacy, inadequate protection from weather conditions, and unsafe movement pathways caused by wet clay soil and poor site planning. Additionally, the absence of lighting, emergency access roads, fire safety measures, and protective boundaries increases protection risks, especially for women and children. The proposed intervention aims to improve public safety, dignity, and living conditions through rehabilitation of WASH facilities, shelter maintenance, drainage and flood mitigation works, waste management, solar lighting installation, awareness campaigns, and site reorganization activities. The plan will also include Cash for Work activities and coordination with WASH and Shelter clusters to ensure effective implementation and community engagement.
